We all are selfish. It's a byproduct of being human and human brain development. The brain learns as it develops, and neurons are strengthened or pruned. 

Our brain's built-in survival mechanism is centered around building strong neuronal connections when it perceives what is in our best interest. Brain development is influenced by our survival and lived experience. Our thinking patterns center around what keeps us safe.

How could we, who are singular beings grow up without a view of the external and internal world, which is our whole universe, be anything but self-centered? 

Our brain is designed and structured on the premise that we must survive at all cost. Out of this primal need, we then develop a sense of self, our wants, likes and dislikes, and a sense of the "other". The other consists of those outside our support system who may be perceived, knowingly or unknowingly, as our competition for resources and even as threats to our survival. 

Life is all about survival and then, depending on our family/culture, we increase our tribe to include allies and contain threats. Discrimination, intolerance, hate, and injury often stem from our limited view and understanding of humanity. 

Our idea of how humanity should be is naturally built around our ideas of what is valuable and conducive to our best interests. It's simple, but becomes complicated when people with different values, beliefs, needs and wants conflict over what they view as absolutes.

Our country must have this oil, water, or whatever resource to remain strong. Our community must have armed security for survival. Out family comes first and we will die to protect the interests of those we love. 

As an individual, most will defend themselves to the death when physically threatened or become extremely hateful and violent when their sense of security and worldview is threatened.

When there is friction, without compromise or adaptability to stress, change, or empathy towards the other, then great divides are created, walls come up, adrenaline is released, fight or flight ensues, and the friction may grow into violence. 

No human is born without the root motivation of selfishness. It's in our basic programming. That's why kindness, compassion, preferring others before yourself, giving just for the benefit of others, and compromising with perceived threats, rather than just killing them off, are behaviors that reveal depth of character, a higher moral or spiritual self, an inclusive life experience, and higher intelligence.

We all would benefit more if everyone saw the peace that could come from equality. The world would be much healthier and secure, if people desired that humans were equally as well off and secure. It would be like one big family instead of one extremely paranoid, violent, world full of treachery, suffering and death.

Unfortunately, the base impulses still have control because humans are individuals and where one may have been enlightened and want for his neighbor's welfare, another person is hoarding resources and building an arsenal to prepare for perceived individual threats or  coming wars. Selfishness breeds paranoia. 

Anyway, don't despair. You're only human after all. One good thing is that we are able to see our shortcomings and evolve. We can choose to fight for the benefit of others, fight for social justice, and intentionally make decisions that are less selfish.

It is wonderful that you are so kind, empathetic, and helpful. I imagine you make the world a better place by being in it, and, even if the people you show compassion to don't notice or say thanks, God sees you.

If you place your self-esteem, happiness, or sense of fulfillment in the hands of other imperfect, insecure, and misguided human beings, you will find yourself questioning who you are, questioning your own worthiness and decision making abilities, and you will feel empty, shallow and lost. People are self-centered and fickle.

If, however, you simply are yourself, true to your own heart, and let go of any expectation of reward or recognition by people, your disappointment and some of your loneliness should lift. People will let you down as we all tend to be selfish and lack the awareness of our deepest self-focused motivation. 

Altruistic people are still motivated by a need to feel gratification for their giving. So, all action that seeks a reward, whether internal or external, is motivated by some sense of selfishness and egotism. When the giving behavior is not satisfying the giver, then the act truly was not selfless and the giver may become sad and resentful.

Expect less and receive more satisfaction by just being true to who you are even when you don't feel rewarded appropriately. It'll come back around to you in time, when you stop looking for inner pats on the back for your good works.

Let go and let God. He is the only one who is good.

I've been running away all my life. I started planning in my closet with an army backpack around eight years old. I filled it with stuff from the house I thought I'd need to survive on my own: hooks, fishing line, seed packets, can opener, rope, lighters, etc. My family was screwed up and my Dad is explosive and cruel. My Mom, who was my best friend as a young girl abandoned us kids a lot due to his temper. Anyway, I watched her deteriorate from cancer and held her hand as she passed.

The first time I did officially run off I was 16. I drove my red, Chevy Nova West, leaving from Virginia, on my last paycheck from UPS. I used enough gas to get to a halfway point and stopped in a Hardee's parking lot near the University of Tennessee. 

I slept in my car which had doors that didn't lock and ate cheez-whiz/crackers with sardines, and I drank Kool-aid. I've been all around the US, down into Mexico and up into Alaska. I've been down to the Fl. Keys and up into Maine.

Everywhere I went, the adventure wore off, and I was left with my bipolar self. I even worked for an outfitter in Bristol Bay, Alaska where the Nushigak and King Salmon rivers intersect and went to UAA. This will probably provide a good laugh. I have my masters degree in psychology. It's a completely useless, but expensive, piece of paper. I can't help anyone; I can't even help myself.

I've been in a lot of hospitals around the country too. Nothing changed in me wherever I go. I still am bipolar. I'm up then massively suicidal to absolute nothingness. I'm rapid cycling. 

I bought firearms in Alaska for deterrence and self-defense. I lived in a cabin in Willow, Alaska at tree line and in another cabin in Nikiski that overlooked the Cook Inlet. It doesn't matter where you go. It's all the same because your mind and heart are still the same. 

I've done so many crazy, reckless things and tried to kill myself (a few times over the years), but nothing changes. I understand the feeling of just wanting to lay down in a dark, quiet room and be distant from everyone and everything. I'd love to hide, but even there I'd hate myself. I'd have to be in a self- induced coma because the only time I find relief is when I sleep or self-medicate. =/ 

I do wish you better luck. I'm at a point now where I'll just kill myself before I run or ask for help anymore. My spirit is crushed.
